messages.author: 138f73570772d624
messages.subject: thermodynamic integration in Stan
parts:
Hi all, 

I was wondering if anyone had implemented the thermodynamic integration for estimating Bayes factors as described in Calderhead & Girolami (2009) (http://dx.doi.org/10.1016/j.csda.2009.07.025). It seems as if it could be useful for something I'm working on, but it has few citations. I would appreciate any thoughts/recommendations people have.

Regards,

Gregory Hunter

messages.author: 138f73570772d624
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] thermodynamic integration in Stan
parts:
Sorry for the slow reply. Thanks for the feedback. I understand why Bayes factors would be deprecated. 

My problem is as follows:

I have interval-censored aggregate usage data and loss numbers for a number of fleets of aircraft. In general, the number of aircraft lost as a function of fleet usage (in flying hours) seems to track as a non-homogeneous Poisson process with a Weibull rate function. The fleets are of similar types of aircraft, but not exactly the same. I would like to make some inferences about this class of aircraft in general and thence about how one ought to plan purchases of additional aircraft. That is, how many spares should one buy? Right now, the variance of my individual fleet estimates are high, especially for the smaller fleets which are of the most interest to me. Since regressions on the individual fleet seem to show some general trends for the model parameters, I want to compare a hierarchical model that allows pooling of information to the non-pooled models. I hope that by doing so I can reduce the variance for the fleets of most interest to me, and create a basis on which to make educated guesses about how a fleet of some new aircraft type would perform.

 I also want to compare various levels and types of fleet pooling to account for various factors, such as relative technological development (old aircraft designs were less reliable) and user peculiarities (if the same aircraft type is used for crop dusting by one user and for mid-altitude long-distance flying by another, their accident rates are likely to be different). 

I had been thinking of a model averaging approach, which is why I was looking at Bayes factors. 

Gregory Hunter

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] thermodynamic integration in Stan
parts:
Thanks for sharing the applied problem.

I'd suggest using something like cross-validation to
evaluate the calibration of the hierarchical model. No
need to calculate Bayes factors if it has narrower posterior
intervals and is well calibrated. (It will almost by definition
at this point have higher log predictive density, which is what
you really care about.)

In a simpler setting, I discuss exactly this evaluation for
hierarchical models and how to code it up in RStan here:

http://mc-stan.org/documentation/case-studies/pool-binary-trials.html

- Bob
